quote: On average, 131 losing tickets will pass such a test for every winner.
content: Conceded: 2<sup>20</sup> is 1,048,576, and 131,115,984 divided by that is 125, not 131. The conclusion the sentence supports is unchanged, since the first ticket to pass the test is still almost certainly a loser, and the essay's other numbers are correct. An arithmetic slip in an illustration is a slip, and the kind of checking the essay recommends is what corrects it.

quote: Suppose you can use another black box to test combinations twice, independently.
content: The condition is in the sentence the note quotes: "test combinations twice, independently." The essay states the independence assumption at the point where it multiplies, as part of the definition of its hypothetical box. The Sally Clark disaster was a failure to ask whether the second death was independent of the first, which is exactly the question the word "independently" raises (Hill 2004). The essay teaches the multiplication together with its condition. The error in the Clark case was dropping the condition.

quote: The larger the space of possibilities in which the hypothesis lies
content: The essay chose the lottery because it has a natural partition. Its claim, that the evidence required grows with the size of the space, holds under any partition: the bits needed to reach a posterior of one half are the negative logarithm of the prior, whatever the prior is. Hájek's paper is titled "The reference class problem is your problem too," and it argues that every interpretation of probability faces the problem (Hájek 2007). It is not an objection peculiar to Bayesian bookkeeping. The sequence's answer to where priors come from is the simplicity prior of Occam's Razor, two essays on. Disagreement does live in the setup, and the essay tells you where it has moved.
